source.title_on_document: Investigating student engagement with personalised generative AI feedback: Effects on creative problem-solving and feedback uptake

supplement.where: Included Appendix, PDF pp. 20-21 (printed pp. 184-185), Tables A1 and A2; referenced on PDF p. 5 (printed p. 169), GenAI feedback conditions. No separate external supplement is identified.
supplement.holds: Table A1 describes personalisation settings and their roles in feedback. Table A2 gives representative prompts and personalised GenAI feedback examples. These appendices contain no additional outcome statistics or standard errors; the condition-comparison results are in main-text Table 2 (PDF p. 11).

paper_design_summary: The analyzed sample comprised 62 Chinese university students who completed product-improvement tasks in a laboratory with both standard ChatGPT-4 feedback and personalised Mr. Ranedeer feedback, with randomized feedback sequence (PDF pp. 4-5 and 8-9, Participants, Procedure and Figure 3). Two trained blinded raters scored the submitted AI-assisted solutions for quality, elaboration and originality; paired Wilcoxon tests compared conditions, but the unit of these analyses and aggregation across solutions are not explicitly reported (PDF pp. 7-8 and 10-11, Measures, Data analysis and Table 2).

assignment.what_was_assigned: Within-person feedback sequence: standard then personalised feedback, or personalised then standard feedback. Figure 3 explicitly labels random assignment and prints N = 31 on each sequence branch. Both sequences receive both AI conditions. The diagram labels the first task PIT 1 and the second PIT 2 in both branches, whereas the Procedure says the other half completed the tasks in the reverse order. Feedback-order randomization is explicit; the actual product/task order and product-by-condition mapping in the second sequence remain ambiguous.
assignment.locator: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 172), Procedure; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Figure 3, image visually inspected.

arms.name: Standard GenAI feedback (ChatGPT-4)
arms.description: General-purpose GPT-4-based chat providing open-ended responses to general prompts and flexible exploration. Every participant experienced this condition in the crossover; its 62 people are the same people as in the personalised condition. Assignment was to feedback sequence, not to one exclusive AI arm. Sources: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 169), GenAI feedback conditions; PDF pp. 8-9 (printed pp. 172-173), Procedure and Figure 3; final sample in PDF pp. 4-5, Participants.

arms.name: Personalised GenAI feedback (Mr. Ranedeer)
arms.description: GPT-4-based Mr. Ranedeer uses configured learner preferences, a personalised learning plan and adaptive feedback/scaffolding. Every participant experienced this condition in the crossover; its 62 people are the same people as in the standard condition. Assignment was to feedback sequence, not to one exclusive AI arm. Sources: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 169), GenAI feedback conditions; PDF pp. 8-9 (printed pp. 172-173), Procedure and Figure 3; Appendix Tables A1-A2, PDF pp. 20-21; final sample in PDF pp. 4-5, Participants.

participants.exclusions: No exclusions, attrition or larger recruitment count are reported. The Participants section explicitly calls 62 the final sample. Figure 3 prints N = 31 at each randomized-sequence branch but no separate aggregate randomized count. In accordance with form-spec rule 1 and its counts field note, the aggregate n_randomized remains null; the two printed sequence counts are retained in assignment.what_was_assigned. The same people contribute to both conditions. No outcome-specific valid-pair counts are printed in Table 2.
participants.who: Chinese students from a normal university, representing diverse academic majors and educational levels; 41 female; ages 18 to 27 years (M = 22.58, SD = 2.53). All but one reported prior GenAI experience. Instructions, task materials and AI interactions were in Chinese. Sources: PDF pp. 4-5 (printed pp. 168-169), Participants.
participants.quote: A total of 62 Chinese university students (41 female) from a normal university participated in the study.
participants.locator: PDF pp. 4-5 (printed pp. 168-169), Method: Participants; final sample statement on PDF p. 5. PDF p. 8 (printed p. 172), Procedure; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Figure 3, image visually inspected.

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT-4 (standard) and Mr. Ranedeer (personalised); both based on GPT-4 architecture. Exact model snapshot not stated (PDF p. 5, printed p. 169, GenAI feedback conditions).
ai_tool.how_used: Participants freely entered prompts and adjusted the interaction flow using the assigned system through the web-based OpenAI interface while producing solutions. Standard ChatGPT-4 provided general suggestions and feedback. Mr. Ranedeer used knowledge level, learning style, tone and communication style to create a learning plan and adapt feedback. It provided heuristic questions and substantive improvement suggestions. Sources: PDF pp. 5-8 (printed pp. 169-172), GenAI feedback conditions, Measures and Procedure; PDF pp. 20-21 (printed pp. 184-185), Appendix Tables A1-A2.

task.description: Torrance product improvement task: propose three original and useful improvements for each of two everyday products, a stuffed bunny and a portable coffee maker, using the assigned GenAI tool. Final responses were submitted in Microsoft Word. Tasks, instructions and AI interactions were in Chinese. Actual product/task order is ambiguous between the Procedure and Figure 3, as recorded in reconciliation. Sources: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 168), Participants; PDF pp. 7-8 (printed pp. 171-172), Measures: CPS performance, Self-efficacy and Procedure; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 173), Figure 3.
task.duration: Mean task completion time: standard feedback 17 minutes (SD = 7); personalised feedback 20 minutes (SD = 6). A 5-minute break separated tasks. No fixed time limit is stated (PDF p. 8, printed p. 172, Procedure).

outcomes.name: Originality of product-improvement solutions
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Originality reflected the novelty of the solutions. Two trained raters, blinded to experimental condition, independently rated all solutions on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = worst, 5 = best). Solutions were presented in randomized order; final scores were averaged across the two raters. Domain-expert credentials are not stated. The within-person condition comparison used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. The paper does not specify how the three requested solutions per task were combined into the analyzed score, or provide outcome-specific valid-pair counts. The analysis unit is unconfirmed and recorded as null: the within-person design alone does not establish what one observation in Table 2 represents. Sources: PDF p. 8 (printed p. 172), Measures: CPS performance; PDF p. 10 (printed p. 174), Data analysis; PDF p. 11 (printed p. 175), Table 2. Within-condition feedback-uptake correlations and regressions on this same outcome are in Tables 4-6, PDF p. 12 (printed p. 176); they are not additional randomized AI contrasts.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: Probable shared sample with c041, Effects of Personalized Generative AI on Student Creativity: Evidence from Creative Performance, Self-efficacy, and Attention Allocation (DOI 10.1007/978-981-95-4499-8_31). This is an inference from matching primary-source reports, not an explicit reuse declaration. Both report 62 students aged 18-27, compatible demographic summaries, the same products and AI systems, the same crossover procedure and condition timings, and identical condition means and SDs for all three creativity dimensions. Neither document confirms the identities or exact number of shared participants. Flag the reports as probable duplicate-sample evidence before pooling; c246 remains lab_rct and retains its own reported statistics.

eligibility.reason: Figure 3 explicitly states random assignment of feedback sequence and shows both orders of standard and personalised GenAI feedback (PDF p. 9, printed p. 173; figure independently viewed). This meets randomized within-person order for an ai_design comparison; both systems use GPT-4 (PDF p. 5, GenAI feedback conditions), and the experiment was conducted in a laboratory (PDF p. 8, Procedure). The final analyzed sample is explicitly 62 people, counted once across repeated conditions, meeting the 50-person threshold (PDF pp. 4-5, Participants; final-sample statement on p. 5). Trained blinded raters scored the submitted solutions for quality, elaboration and originality, produced using the assigned AI (PDF pp. 7-8, Measures and Procedure). The unreported analysis unit, solution-aggregation rule and outcome-specific valid-pair counts concern extraction and precision; the explicit final sample and output ratings support criteria 2 and 3. The ambiguous product/task order does not overturn Figure 3's explicit feedback-order randomization. Probable c041 sample overlap requires duplicate-sample handling and does not change these three eligibility judgments.

one_line_finding: Personalised versus standard GenAI feedback yielded higher solution quality (3.50 vs 3.08, p = .001) and elaboration (3.58 vs 2.48, p < .001), with no clear originality difference (2.92 vs 3.13, p = 0.098; PDF p. 11, printed p. 175, Table 2).
open_questions: What is one observation in the Table 2 analyses, how were the three solutions requested per task aggregated into each analyzed score, and how many valid participant pairs entered each outcome test? The paper states averaging across raters but not aggregation across solutions, and does not print outcome-specific sample sizes; the outcome units are therefore null (PDF p. 8, printed p. 172, Measures; p. 10, printed p. 174, Data analysis; p. 11, printed p. 175, Table 2).

What was the actual product/task order and product-by-feedback mapping in the second randomized sequence? Procedure says the other half completed the tasks in the reverse order, whereas Figure 3 labels PIT 1 then PIT 2 in both branches and reverses feedback. Clarification of whether PIT labels indicate products or periods, or a corrected procedure description, is missing (PDF pp. 8-9, printed pp. 172-173).

Do c246 and c041 report the same experimental participants, and what is the exact overlap? Matching demographics, methods, task timings and creativity means/SDs strongly support probable overlap, but neither paper explicitly confirms shared participant identities or their number. Author confirmation is needed for sample deduplication and primary-record selection (c246 PDF pp. 4-5, 7-8 and 11; c041 PDF pp. 4-8).
notes: Reconciled on 2026-10-09 from both valid raw forms. The entire markdown conversion was read in consecutive chunks, including references and Appendix. Numerical entries were checked against the PDF using PyMuPDF text extraction; Table 2 was also checked with text-based table extraction. Figure 3 was extracted and viewed in memory because its assignment label and branch counts are absent from the text layer. No derived effect sizes, standard errors, total output counts or aggregate randomized count were calculated. PDF locators are one-based and distinguish printed journal pages. Arms and outcomes were matched by meaning, not list position or outcome ID: both forms contain the same three outcomes and identical Table 2 statistics. The final outcome IDs follow A, with novelty first under the codebook hierarchy; this ordering does not assert a paper-designated primary outcome. Neither the paper nor a preregistration designates one CPS dimension as primary. The three outcomes are immediate with-AI scores; no across-person diversity or unassisted after-AI outcome is reported. Table 2 prints negative Wilcoxon z and negative Cohen’s r for all dimensions; these signs and confidence intervals are preserved exactly. Direction is based on the reported arm means and comparisons. No paired-difference SD, paired-outcome correlation or SE for the AI-condition contrast is supplied. The same final sample contributes to both conditions; arm counts must not be added. The explicit final sample count supports eligibility, while outcome-specific valid-pair counts and aggregation across solutions remain unreported. Self-efficacy is a self-report covariate (PDF pp. 8 and 10). Feedback uptake and interaction codes measure the collaboration process rather than creativity or diversity of the submitted products (PDF pp. 9-13, Tables 1, 3 and 7, Figure 4); these are excluded from the outcome inventory. Tables 4-6 analyze associations with the same CPS outcomes rather than additional randomized AI contrasts. Appendix Tables A1-A2 add tool settings and examples, not outcomes or precision estimates. No preregistration, explicit participant-reuse declaration or study data/analysis-code release is stated in c246. Cross-document evidence now supports probable participant overlap with c041, as detailed in sample_overlap. The Mr. Ranedeer GitHub URL on PDF p. 5 is the intervention source rather than a study repository. The comparison covered design, assignment, arms, participant counts, AI tool and role, task, all outcome fields and statistics/locators, supplement, sample overlap, company involvement, all eligibility criteria and the finding. Two substantive differences are recorded below. Synonymous wording, arm/outcome ordering, empty versus not_stated overlap coding, and corrupted punctuation in the raw forms are not counted as substantive differences. Shared reporting gaps are retained in open_questions; n_unresolved counts unresolved differences between forms only. Finalized on 2026-10-09 after independently reading the complete c246 markdown, including its Appendix, and the complete c041 markdown, including its references. Relevant source passages and every added numerical comparison were checked with PyMuPDF text extraction; c246 Table 2 was also checked with table extraction, and Figure 3 was extracted and visually inspected in memory. Both challenge problems were corrected: all three outcome units are now null because the analytical observation is not explicitly established, and probable c041 sample overlap is recorded with cross-document evidence. Null is used for the unconfirmed analysis unit rather than selecting an unsupported substantive unit from the form vocabulary. All c246 outcome statistics, participant counts, design class and the already-complete source.supplement are retained. The reconciliation object is preserved unchanged as the prior audit record; its participant-unit and overlap decisions are superseded by the final challenge resolutions. The aggregation/unit/valid-pair question, the task-order question shared by open_questions and the unresolved reconciliation difference, and the exact-overlap question are classified in final.open_items. None changes a documented eligibility criterion. The final resolution counts count challenge problems; retained reporting questions are listed separately in final.open_items.

open_items.item: open_questions[0]: Table 2 analysis unit, aggregation across the requested solutions and outcome-specific valid-pair counts remain unreported. Author scoring and analysis documentation with valid-pair counts would settle this. It affects extraction and precision; criteria 2 and 3 are supported by the explicit final analyzed sample of 62 (PDF p. 5, Participants) and direct solution ratings (PDF pp. 7-8, Measures).

open_questions[1] and unresolved reconciliation.differences[1]: the actual product/task order and product-by-feedback mapping in the second sequence remain ambiguous between Procedure and Figure 3 (PDF pp. 8-9). An author-confirmed protocol or corrected procedure description would settle this. Criterion 1 remains met because Figure 3 explicitly randomizes feedback sequence.

open_questions[2]: exact participant overlap between c246 and c041 remains unconfirmed despite the matching primary-source reports (c246 PDF pp. 4-5, 7-8 and 11; c041 PDF pp. 4-8). Author confirmation of cohort identity and the number shared would settle sample deduplication and primary-record selection. This does not change any of the three study-level eligibility criteria.
